acts.title: Text A · Nine days without a door
text: Until I was thirty-one I used to take the same holiday every year. Same coast, same hotel, same four restaurants. I told myself I was being sensible. I was being frightened, which is a different thing.

What changed it was a conversation I did not enjoy. A friend asked me, quite pleasantly, when I had last done something I was not already good at. I could not answer. Two months later we were on a bus in northern Kyrgyzstan with everything we owned on our backs.

The first two days were miserable. I was not fit, I had brought the wrong boots, and I discovered that I am extremely bad at roughing it. On the third day we came over a ridge and the whole valley opened underneath us, and I stopped complaining. I did not start again for six days.
We saw four people in five days. It was the most remote place I had ever stood in, and the quietest.

items.q: Why did the writer always take the same holiday?
o: Fear, although at the time it looked like being sensible

items.q: What changed the writer’s mind?
o: A question from a friend that they could not answer

acts.title: Text B · What I got wrong, and what it was worth
text: I got three things wrong, and I would get two of them wrong again.
The boots were a genuine mistake. I bought them the week before and did not wear them in, and by the second afternoon I was walking on something that no longer felt like a foot.
The second mistake was the food. We were carrying nine days of it, and I had packed for the person I wished I were rather than the person who gets hungry at eleven in the morning.

The third was the phone, and this one I do not regret. There was no signal for the whole trek. I had been dreading it. In fact it was the part that changed something: for the first time in years I was not carrying a small responsibility in my pocket.
Would I do it again? I was determined never to, for about a fortnight. Then I started looking at maps.

items.s: The writer had worn the boots in before the trip.
They packed less food than they actually needed.
The writer regrets having no phone signal.
There was no signal for the whole trek.
Immediately afterwards the writer wanted to go again.

acts.title: Look again at the two texts
text: Until I was thirty-one I used to take the same holiday every year.
Two months later we were on a bus with everything we owned on our backs.
On the third day we came over a ridge and the whole valley opened underneath us.
I bought them the week before and did not wear them in.
I had been dreading it.
It was the most remote place I had ever stood in.

items.q: “I used to take the same holiday every year.” What does used to describe?
o: A repeated habit that has now stopped

items.q: “we came over a ridge and the whole valley opened” — which form is this?
o: Past simple, for the events that move the story on

items.q: “It was the most remote place I had ever stood in.” Why the past perfect here?
o: It reaches back before the moment of the story

items.q: Which form gives the background rather than the events?
o: I was not fit, I had brought the wrong boots

acts.title: The three forms a story runs on
rule: A narrative in English uses three past forms, and each one does a different job. Getting the job right is what makes a story easy to follow; using only the past simple makes it flat, and using the wrong one makes it confusing.
points: The events. What happened, in the order it happened. This is the backbone of any story.
The background. What was already going on when those events happened.
Habits and states before the story starts. States take used to only: would describes repeated actions, never states.
Anything that reaches back further still. Lesson 10 takes this apart properly.
eg: We came over a ridge and the valley opened underneath us.
Past simple — two events, in order.
I was driving and Liz was reading the map.
Past continuous — the background situation.
While I was reading the map, we missed the turning.
Long action interrupted by a short one.
I used to take the same holiday every year.
A habit that has stopped.
There used to be a café at the top of that path.
A past state — would is impossible here.
Every morning we would set off before six.
A repeated past action. would works, and sounds slightly literary.
I bought the boots the week before.
Past simple with a stated finished time.
It was the most remote place I had ever stood in.
Past perfect, reaching back before the story.
We were crawling along and I was beginning to get nervous.
Two background actions running together.
I had been dreading it.
Past perfect continuous — duration, before the story’s present.
acts.careful: “There would be a café at the top” does not mean the same as “There used to be a café at the top.” With states — be, have, know, like — only used to works.

write.q: Write about 180 words on a time you did something you were not comfortable with — a journey, a move, a job, a performance. Use the past continuous at least twice for the background, used to at least once for how things had been before, and the past simple throughout for the events. End with what you think of it now.
write.model:
Until I was about twenty-six I used to turn down anything that involved speaking in front of people. There used to be a standard excuse, and I used it perhaps forty times.

What changed it was a colleague going into hospital two days before a conference. Nobody else knew the material. I said yes at four in the afternoon and regretted it by five.

I spent the next thirty-six hours writing a script and learning it, which turned out to be exactly the wrong preparation. While I was waiting at the side of the room, the chair changed the running order and cut my slot from thirty minutes to twelve. The script was useless. I was shaking, the projector was not working, and about ninety people were watching somebody fix it.

So I talked instead. It was the first time I had spoken without notes, and it was easily the best thing I had done that year.

Looking back, the accident was the whole point. Nothing prepared would have taught me that.
